In an eager execution model, every kernel launch involves significant CPU work, including argument validation, memory management checks, and the generation of hardware commands that are sent to the GPU via the driver. When executing a deep neural network or a complex simulation with hundreds of small kernels, this per-launch latency can dominate the execution time, causing the GPU to sit idle waiting for the CPU to issue the next command. A CUDA Graph captures this entire sequence of operations once, creating a static DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) of nodes. During replay, the CPU simply issues a single command to the GPU to execute the pre-built graph, allowing the GPU’s internal scheduler to stream kernels back-to-back with minimal CPU intervention. This effectively hides the launch latency and maximizes GPU utilization, particularly for workloads with short kernel durations.

The primary reason CUDA graph replay outperforms eager kernel launching is the drastic reduction in host-device synchronization overhead and API call latency. In an eager execution model, every kernel launch requires the CPU to prepare command buffers, validate parameters, and submit work to the GPU driver through multiple expensive API calls (such as `cudaLaunchKernel`). This process involves significant CPU-side overhead, context switches, and driver processing. By contrast, a CUDA graph captures these operations into a single, pre-compiled execution plan stored in memory. When replayed, the entire sequence is submitted to the GPU in one atomic operation, essentially bypassing the per-kernel CPU overhead and allowing the GPU to start executing almost immediately.

Additionally, CUDA graphs enable the GPU to optimize the internal scheduling and memory management of the captured kernels. Because the graph is static, the driver can pre-allocate resources and determine optimal execution order without the uncertainty present in dynamic, eager execution. This is particularly beneficial for deep learning workloads or simulation steps that involve thousands of small, tightly coupled kernels, where the CPU launch latency would otherwise dominate the actual computation time, creating "bubbles" in the GPU's pipeline.
